sentences.text: The genus name Ornithoprion translates from Greek as 'bird saw', a reference to its bird-like skull and saw-like lower jaw teeth.
The specific name hertwigi honors the German zoologist Oscar Hertwig.
Ornithoprion was small relative to its order, possessing a cranium up to 10 cm long and an estimated total body length of approximately 91 cm.
Most known specimens are preserved on their side and are flattened, a condition that includes the holotype.
The mandibular rostrum articulated with the Meckel's cartilages at a flexible joint.
The genus Ornithoprion was described by Rainer Zangerl in 1966.
The only known species, Ornithoprion hertwigi, lived during the Moscovian stage of the Pennsylvanian subperiod.
Fossils of Ornithoprion are preserved in black shales from the area that is now the Midwestern United States.
Specimen FMNH PF-2710 from the Mecca Quarry was designated as the holotype of the species.
The rounded shape of Ornithoprion's teeth suggests it hunted hard-shelled invertebrates.
Bite marks and damage on some fossils indicate that Ornithoprion was preyed upon by other carnivores.
Ornithoprion is believed to have been durophagous, feeding on shelled invertebrates.
The rounded, bulbous crowns of Ornithoprion's tooth whorl were likely adaptations for crushing shelled prey.
Ornithoprion is classified in the order Eugeneodontiformes and the family Caseodontidae, though its classification has been debated due to its unique anatomy.
Ornithoprion is a distant relative of living sharks, despite sometimes being referred to as a shark.
Ornithoprion was originally classified in the family Edestidae, which was traditionally placed in the order Bradyodonti or the subclass Holocephali.
Zangerl originally classified Ornithoprion and other edestids as elasmobranchs.
While Zangerl's family and order classifications are still used, his view that eugeneodonts are elasmobranchs has been refuted; they are now considered a monophyletic group within Holocephali.
Ornithoprion lived during the Carboniferous period approximately 315.2 million years ago.
Ornithoprion fossils were found in deposits from the North American Midcontinent Sea, a large inland sea.
While Zangerl speculated that processes on the back of the cranium were a fused hyoid arch, this interpretation has been questioned by paleontologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen.

There is a debate regarding the attachment of Ornithoprion's upper teeth, with some researchers suggesting they attached to the underside of the cranium while others believe they attached to a fused portion of the palatoquadrates.

Roger S. Miles tentatively placed Ornithoprion in Holocephali but suggested its similarities to edestids resulted from convergent evolution due to differences in gill anatomy, tooth histology, and palatoquadrates.
